pages.summary: Run a block when a condition holds, with optional elseif and else branches.
body: The branches are tried in order and the first whose condition holds runs; `else` runs when none does. A condition holds when it is not empty and every one of its elements is nonzero, so `if [1 1 0]` does not run its block, and `if []` never does. Use `any` or `all` to say which is meant for an array.
syntax: if condition, statements, end
Runs the statements when the condition holds.
if condition, statements, elseif other, statements, else, statements, end
Tries each condition in turn; `else` takes everything left.
inputs: Usually a comparison (`x > 0`), a test such as `isempty(s)`, or a combination with `&&` and `||`, which stop as soon as the answer is known.

examples.title: Three branches
examples.code:
x = -3;
if x > 0
    disp('positive')
elseif x < 0
    disp('negative')
else
    disp('zero')
end

examples.title: A condition on an array holds only if every element holds
examples.intro: `all` and `any` say which of the two you mean.
examples.code:
v = [2 5 -1];
if v > 0
    disp('all positive')
else
    disp('not all positive')
end
if any(v < 0)
    fprintf('%d of them negative\n', nnz(v < 0))
end
examples.output:
not all positive
1 of them negative

examples.title: Short-circuit tests
examples.intro: `&&` does not evaluate its right side when the left is false, so the index is only tried when there is an element.
examples.code:
s = [];
if ~isempty(s) && s(1) == 0
    disp('starts with zero')
else
    disp('empty, or does not start with zero')
end
examples.output: empty, or does not start with zero

pages.summary: Repeat a block once for each column of an array.
body: The loop variable takes each column of the array in turn: for a row vector such as `1:n`, each element. Changing the loop variable inside the block does not change the next pass, and after the loop it keeps its last value. `break` leaves the loop and `continue` goes on to the next pass.
syntax: for k = first:last, statements, end
`k` takes the values first, first+1, …, last.
for k = first:step:last, statements, end
Steps of `step`, which may be negative or not whole.
for column = A, statements, end
Each column of `A` in turn (a column vector of a matrix; a cell of a cell row).

examples.title: A running total
Counting down in steps
examples.code:
for t = 1:-0.25:0
    fprintf('%.2f ', t)
end
fprintf('\n')

examples.title: The columns of a matrix
examples.intro: Each pass gets a whole column.
examples.code:
A = [1 2 3; 4 5 6];
for c = A
    disp(c')
end

examples.title: Growing a result row by row

pages.summary: Repeat a block for as long as a condition holds.
body: The condition is tested before each pass, so the block may never run. As with `if`, an array condition holds only when every element is nonzero. Make sure something in the block changes the condition, or use `break`; Ctrl+C stops a loop that runs on.
syntax: while condition, statements, end
Runs the statements again and again while the condition holds.

examples.title: Halving until small
Newton's method for a square root
examples.intro: The loop stops when a step changes the answer by less than a tolerance.

pages.summary: Pick a block by comparing a value with cases (numbers or text).
body: The value is compared with each `case` in turn and the first that matches runs; `otherwise` runs when none does. Numbers match when they are equal, text when it is the same text. A case given as a cell array, such as `{'png', 'jpg'}`, matches any of its members. Only one block runs: there is no falling through to the next case.
syntax: switch value, case a, statements, case {b, c}, statements, otherwise, statements, end
Runs the block of the first case that matches `value`.

examples.title: Cases of text
examples.code:
ext = 'jpg';
switch ext
    case {'png', 'jpg', 'gif'}
        disp('an image')
    case 'txt'
        disp('text')
    otherwise
        disp('something else')
end

examples.title: Cases of numbers
examples.code:
for n = 1:4
    switch mod(n, 3)
        case 0
            fprintf('%d: divisible by 3\n', n)
        case 1
            fprintf('%d: one more than a multiple of 3\n', n)
        otherwise
            fprintf('%d: two more\n', n)
    end
end
examples.output:
1: one more than a multiple of 3
2: two more
3: divisible by 3
4: one more than a multiple of 3

pages.summary: Run a block, and another block if the first one throws an error.
body: When a statement in the `try` block throws an error, the rest of that block is skipped and the `catch` block runs; without an error the `catch` block is passed over. Named after `catch`, the error is an exception whose `message`, `identifier` and `stack` say what went wrong. `rethrow` passes it on, and `error` throws one of your own.
syntax: try, statements, catch, statements, end
Runs the catch block if the try block fails.
try, statements, catch err, statements, end
The same, with the error in `err`.

examples.title: Catching an error and reading its message
examples.output: Index exceeds the number of array elements. Index must not exceed 3.

examples.title: A fallback when something fails
examples.intro: `str2double` gives `NaN` for text that is not a number; `error` makes the failure explicit, and the catch block supplies a default.
examples.output:
Not a number: twelve; using 0
v =

     0

pages.summary: Start a function: in a function file, or after the code of a script file.
body: A function has its own workspace: it sees only its inputs, and the caller sees only its outputs. A file whose first code is a function is a function file, called by the file's name; more functions after the first are local to the file. A script file may end with local functions too, as may the code typed at the prompt. Each function ends with `end`, or with the next function line when no function in the file uses `end`.
syntax: function y = name(x)
One input and one output.
function [a, b] = name(x, y)
Several outputs, in brackets; the caller takes as many as it asks for (`nargout` says how many).
function name(varargin)
Any number of inputs, in the cell array `varargin` (`nargin` counts them).

examples.title: A function after the code that calls it
Two outputs
A default for an input left out
examples.intro: `nargin` is how many inputs the call gave.
examples.code:
greet('Ada')
greet()

function greet(name)
    if nargin < 1
        name = 'world';
    end
    fprintf('Hello, %s!\n', name)
end
